clue.text: Dickensian fellow's turned informer

indicators.note: turned tells us to read the fellow's word from right to left

parts.note: a fellow of a college is a don; with the possessive s that gives DONS
a grass is slang for a police informer

explanation.surface: A character out of Dickens has become a police snitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' reverses DONS to SNOD. Augustus Snodgrass is the would-be poet of Dickens's The Pickwick Papers.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs to a member of the Pickwick Club, a character created by Charles Dickens.

clue.text: See 30
Roughly two years old, English bit of lacework

indicators.note: roughly, as in done without care, says these letters are to be jumbled

parts.note: Y is the abbreviation for year, so two years give two Ys

explanation.surface: A piece of lace is said to be about two years old and English made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roughly' looks like it qualifies 'two years' as an approximate age, but it is the anagram signal for Y, Y, OLD and E. It also points at Mrs Doyle of Father Ted, the puzzle's theme.
explanation.definitionFit: A doyley is a variant spelling of doily, a small ornamental mat of lace or paper.

clue.text: Man overboard? That's a new recruit

parts.note: read as a man over a board: a chessman on the board, here the castle piece
that is gives i.e., the abbreviation for id est

explanation.surface: A sailor falls into the sea, and the speaker remarks that he must be a beginner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man overboard?' sounds like a cry at sea, but the question mark invites the reading 'a man over a board', i.e. a chess piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A rookie is an inexperienced newcomer, especially a raw recruit to the army or police.

clue.text: New church in southern Ireland's losing ground, honest

indicators.note: in says the new church goes inside the shortened country
losing says one word is taken out of the country's name

parts.note: the country's name, its possessive s read as 'is'
ground means land, the part of the name that goes
CE stands for the Church of England

explanation.surface: A new church is being built in southern Ireland, where farmland is disappearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ground' looks like soil but means LAND, which 'losing' strips from the country; 'in' then sets the new church inside what is left, all after S.
explanation.definitionFit: Sincere means genuine and truthful in feeling, a synonym for honest.

clue.text: "Dips won't run out" (from the sign outside)

indicators.note: outside says the musical abbreviation goes around the jumbled letters

parts.note: D.S., dal segno, is the musical direction meaning 'from the sign'

indicators.note: out, meaning wrong or not in place, says the letters of won't run are rearranged

explanation.surface: A roadside notice warns that the dips in the road will not wash away.
explanation.walkthrough: D.S. (dal segno) is the musical instruction to repeat from the sign. 'out' scrambles the letters of won't run, and 'outside' wraps the D.S. around them.
explanation.definitionFit: Downturns are declines or dips, as in the economy or in a road surface.

clue.text: Sort of doormen employed by pub — the heavily built type

indicators.note: sort, as a verb, means rearrange, so the letters of doormen are reordered

parts.note: PH, short for public house, is the map abbreviation for a pub

explanation.surface: Some bouncers working at a pub are big, burly men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of' looks like it qualifies 'doormen', but it signals an anagram of that word; 'employed by' just joins on the pub.
explanation.definitionFit: In old body-type theory, an endomorph has a soft, rounded, heavily built physique.

clue.text: Usual price to enter jar

parts.note: to enter is to go in
jar as a verb means grate, to irritate or sound harshly

explanation.surface: Someone asks what it normally costs to get into a jar.
explanation.definitionFit: The going rate is the standard or prevailing charge for something.

clue.text: Three eejits? So said 27's 17 down 3, endlessly!

parts.note: an eejit is an Irish idiot, a goon; three of them give the word three times
an eejit is an Irish idiot, a goon; three of them give the word three times
an eejit is an Irish idiot, a goon; three of them give the word three times

explanation.surface: Three Irish fools are quoted as being what a famous housekeeper kept saying.
explanation.walkthrough: 27 is FATHER TED, 17 down is MRS and 3 is DOYLEY; DOYLEY without its last letter gives Mrs Doyle, the show's housekeeper, whose catchphrase this is.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is Mrs Doyle's repeated urging in the sitcom, so the cross-referenced description names it.

clue.text: Enough dry ground for a thin runner

indicators.note: ground, the past tense of grind, says the letters are crushed and reformed

explanation.surface: The going is firm enough for a lean racer to run.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ground' looks like a noun after 'dry' but is the anagram signal for ENOUGH DRY.
explanation.definitionFit: A greyhound is a lean, slender racing dog, so it fits a thin runner.

clue.text: See 9
Adore snacks? "X" marked the spot where these appear

definitions.text: "X" marked the spot where these appear

parts.note: to adore is to love
bites are small snacks

explanation.surface: A treasure-map motto is turned into a hint about where marks appear on the skin.
explanation.walkthrough: X is the conventional sign for a kiss, so a kiss marked the spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Love bites are bruises left on the skin by passionate kissing, appearing where the kiss landed.

clue.text: See 23
Scabs left in some beastly panto costume

indicators.note: in says the abbreviation for left goes inside the costume

parts.note: a pantomime horse has a front half and a back half, the back legs

explanation.surface: Strike-breakers are dressed up as an animal in a pantomime.
explanation.walkthrough: In British pantomime (a Christmas stage show) a horse or cow costume is worn by two actors, one playing the back legs.
explanation.definitionFit: Blacklegs and scabs are both derogatory names for workers who break a strike.

clue.text: Poetaster's garbled works produced by 3 23, say?

indicators.note: garbled means mixed up, so the letters of the clue word are rearranged

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: A bad poet's muddled writings are put on by a theatrical producer.
explanation.walkthrough: 3 23 is DOYLEY CARTES, which suggests D'Oyly Carte, the company that staged Gilbert and Sullivan's comic operas.
explanation.definitionFit: Operettas are light comic operas, as produced by the D'Oyly Carte company.

clue.text: Current accommodation in area by bank

parts.note: a river is a current of water
a flat is a type of living accommodation

explanation.surface: A waterside apartment is described as standing near the bank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' and 'bank' look financial, but one is a flowing stream and the other its edge.
explanation.definitionFit: A river flat is a stretch of low, level ground alongside a river.

clue.text: Some licks from a Gibson? On the contrary

indicators.note: from says the name is taken out of the words before it, read as a hidden run

explanation.surface: A guitarist's riffs played on a Gibson guitar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the contrary' flips the clue to read 'a Gibson from some licks': MEL is hidden in soME Licks. Mel Gibson is the actor.
explanation.definitionFit: Mel Gibson is a famous actor, so Mel is a Gibson by surname.

clue.text: Wife hit in the ear by Victorian writer

parts.note: a wife is styled Mrs

indicators.note: in the ear says the word is as heard, not as spelt

parts.note: hit means beaten

explanation.surface: A Victorian author is said to have struck his wife on the ear.
explanation.walkthrough: BEETON is heard like BEATEN. Mrs Beeton wrote the famous Book of Household Management (1861).
explanation.definitionFit: Isabella Beeton was a Victorian author of a best-selling household cookery book.

clue.text: What got old Sid somewhat spaced out?

definitions.text: What got old Sid somewhat spaced out?

indicators.note: spaced out means taking letters with gaps between them, every other one of old Sid

explanation.surface: A question about the drug that left a punk rocker hallucinating.
explanation.walkthrough: Every other letter of oLd SiD gives LSD. Sid Vicious of the Sex Pistols suits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: LSD is a hallucinogenic drug that makes users spaced out; it is also old British money.

clue.text: Italian who painted the Queen as more saucy

parts.note: Filippo Lippi was an Italian Renaissance painter
ER is the royal cipher of Queen Elizabeth

explanation.surface: An Italian old master portrayed the monarch as rather cheeky.
explanation.definitionFit: Lippy is informal for impudent or cheeky, so lippier is a comparative of saucy.

clue.text: Playing area used by batters and pitchers

indicators.note: used by says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A ground where baseball players bat and pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: The baseball surface suggests a field, but the run is in batterS AND PITchers.
explanation.definitionFit: A sandpit is an area filled with sand where children play.

clue.text: The German's backed down

indicators.note: backed means going backwards, so the German word is reversed

parts.note: das is the German neuter article meaning 'the'; the 's is read as 'is'

explanation.surface: A German is said to have retreated in low spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling down is a common idiom for feeling unhappy or sad.

clue.text: A china vase last dropped by dilettante

parts.note: in cockney rhyming slang china plate means mate

indicators.note: last dropped says the final letter of the vase word goes

parts.note: an urn is a type of vase

explanation.surface: A dabbler has let a porcelain vase fall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'china' looks like porcelain but is rhyming slang: china plate = mate. 'last dropped' cuts the N from URN.
explanation.definitionFit: A dilettante dabbles in an art without professional training, an amateur.

clue.text: Cooked just our race day menus

indicators.note: cooked, as in cooked up, says the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Dishes prepared for a meal on the day of a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooked' suits the menu surface but is the anagram signal for JUSTOURRACE plus D.
explanation.definitionFit: A carte du jour is a menu of the day, so its plural means menus.

clue.text: Get less time in the kitchen area

indicators.note: in says the time abbreviation goes inside the kitchen fixture

parts.note: the sink is an area of a kitchen
HR is the abbreviation for hour, a measure of time

explanation.surface: An instruction to spend less time cooking.
explanation.definitionFit: To shrink is to become smaller in size or amount.

clue.text: Vessel at base in Irish town

parts.note: an ark is a vessel, as Noah's
at base, at the bottom, means low

explanation.surface: A ship is moored at a naval base in an Irish port.
explanation.walkthrough: Arklow is a harbour town in County Wicklow, Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Arklow is a coastal town in County Wicklow in the Republic of Ireland.

clue.text: See 17
Plump for new 3-D TV series

parts.note: plump means fat

indicators.note: new says the letters of the spelled-out 3-D are made afresh

parts.note: read as three and D, giving the letters THREED

explanation.surface: Someone opts for a new three-dimensional television show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plump for' looks like 'choose', but Plump is FAT. 'new' rearranges THREED to HERTED. The series is the 1990s Channel 4 sitcom about Irish priests.
explanation.definitionFit: Father Ted was a celebrated Channel 4 sitcom set on Craggy Island.

clue.text: Excused 27 dropping the …

definitions.meaning: the sitcom's title without the word 'the' leaves a slang word for breaking wind, which is what this phrase also means

explanation.surface: Someone pardoned is being pinned on the sitcom.
explanation.walkthrough: FATHER TED minus THE leaves FARTED, and to fart is to let off. The ellipsis leads on to the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To let off means to excuse from punishment and, slangily, to break wind.

clue.text: … good humour put back in, eg by tipsy laity

indicators.note: put back says the two words before it are reversed together
tipsy, slightly drunk, says the letters of laity are jumbled

explanation.surface: Good cheer returns, for example, among drunken churchgoers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put back' turns IN EG into GENI, and 'tipsy' rearranges LAITY to ALITY.
explanation.definitionFit: Geniality is a friendly, cheerful disposition, a synonym of good humour.

clue.text: Wrong or right to hang man who acted in 27?

indicators.note: wrong, as in in error, says the letters are put in a different order

explanation.surface: A debate over whether hanging a man is wrong or right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrong or right' looks like a moral question, but Wrong is the anagram signal for OR, R and TO HANG MAN. Graham Norton played Father Noel Furlong.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish TV presenter played the hyperactive priest Father Noel Furlong in the sitcom, so he is one who acted in it.

clue.text: Rob winked mischievously, having 28

indicators.note: mischievously, as in up to tricks, says these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Rob gave a cheeky wink, having been excused.
explanation.walkthrough: 28 is LET OFF, in its windy sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To break wind is to let off, so 'having 28' means having farted.
